title: Japan’s monetary research volume examines how overseas shocks reach domestic prices and markets
summary: A foreign investor’s need for cash can move Japanese asset prices even when the underlying Japanese issuer has received little new economic information. The November issue of Monetary and Economic Studies provides direct evidence for this channel in a study of foreign open-end funds. Other contributions consider how supply disruptions pass into inflation, why central bank independence matters during such episodes, and whether electronic cash could operate without a transaction ledger. The five texts include a conference summary, two of its speeches and two research papers. Their conclusions belong to the individual authors and speakers.

Kenta Yamamoto, Tomohiro Okubo, Nobuhiro Abe and Yukio Minoura examine overseas-domiciled funds with Japanese holdings. Across historical periods of global market stress and rising foreign policy rates, redemptions at such funds sometimes led them to sell Japanese assets. In March 2020, mixed bond funds sold primarily Japanese government bonds. Their liquidity made them a potential source of cash even when investors were reacting to stress elsewhere. The study distinguishes the evidence on which securities funds sold from a separate estimate of how trades by market participants can affect aggregate equity and listed real estate investment trust prices.

Table 4 of the fund study estimates aggregate demand multipliers of roughly three for equities and five for REITs. In the authors’ interpretation, an exogenous purchase equivalent to 1% of the equity market is associated with an increase of about 3% in its aggregate price level. The estimate uses sector-specific flows after controlling for common shocks. Its magnitude depends on identification, sector definitions and controls. The coefficient does not turn a particular fund’s redemption into a forecast loss, especially when cash buffers, dealer participation or the mix of securities sold differ from the estimation sample. The bond sales evidence also does not establish the same price multiplier for government bonds.

Governor Kazuo Ueda’s opening remarks make a parallel distinction between an external impulse and domestic propagation. Higher oil prices in the mid-2000s reduced real income without a sustained upward shift in Japanese wages or expectations. From around 2021, the cost shock was broader, yen depreciation amplified it and persistent labour shortages changed bargaining conditions. Firms passed on more costs and workers became more willing to seek wage increases. Medium- to long-term inflation expectations nevertheless rose only modestly from their previously low levels, with readings varying across measures (opening remarks, chart 5). The conference summary also reports different perspectives on supply shocks, expectations, fiscal conditions and the limits of policy models. It records debate rather than a collective Board forecast.

In the Mayekawa Lecture, Donald Kohn argued that defending central bank independence requires performance against statutory objectives, flexibility when evidence changes and accountability to elected representatives. He distinguished explaining the consequences of an unsustainable fiscal path from choosing how a government should close a budget gap. His argument about debt and political pressure concerns institutional incentives. It provides no estimate of a Japanese term premium.

Yuko Tamura and co-authors separately examine a payment design in which users exchange electronic cash without relying on a central transaction ledger. Smartphone tests showed that sending and receiving could be practical under the examined conditions. The authors measured the transaction response, excluding application operations and time to establish device connections. Identity verification, oversight, compliance and deployment remained open questions. The work therefore documents one possible operational design. It provides neither an adoption forecast nor an announcement of a Bank of Japan payment instrument.

questions.question: Which Japanese holdings would foreign funds sell first in a new liquidity squeeze?
questions.detail: The fund paper documents sales of liquid government bonds and estimates equity and REIT price sensitivity separately. Examine portfolio holdings, cash buffers, redemption terms, fund domicile and the depth of dealer markets at the relevant date. Separate sales to meet withdrawals from transactions prompted by new information about Japan. Assuming that all redemptions produce proportionate sales of every asset could materially misstate hedge performance.

questions.question: How robust are the estimated equity and REIT price effects outside the paper’s sample?
questions.detail: The authors use aggregate sector shocks and common-factor controls. Compare estimates under alternative sector groupings, liquidity regimes and identification choices, and examine the uncertainty around the multipliers. Holding-period investors need to understand both the initial price response and the speed of any reversal. The estimate alone does not measure realised trading costs or give a duration for the repricing.

questions.question: What would indicate that a new import-price shock was changing wage and pricing norms?
questions.detail: Ueda distinguishes episodes by the exchange rate, breadth of the shock and labour-market conditions. Compare underlying service inflation, wage settlements, firms’ price plans and expectations by horizon with contemporaneous import prices. Tracking whether these indicators move together could help assess whether an oil-driven change in market inflation compensation would persist after the initial shock faded.
